960.title: Ain Jalut, 1260
960.hook: the Mamluks of Egypt stop the Mongol advance in Palestine
960.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Talut and Jalut in surah al-Baqarah, and its line that Allah is with the steadfast is often quoted in times of hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baghdad, the city of the caliphs, sacked, and a river the chronicles say ran dark with ink. Your line was: the river of ink. Which book did you look after? Day nine hundred sixty.

A letter arrives in Cairo. It comes from the Mongol camp, and the chronicles say it demands surrender, with threats to match. Baghdad has fallen. The cities of Syria have fallen or opened their gates. The sultan of Egypt, a soldier named Qutuz, has to answer. He could pay. He could wait behind the walls and hope. Instead, the chronicles say, he gathers his army and marches north, out of Egypt, to meet them. The two armies come face to face beside a spring in Palestine, a spring with a name out of an old story. Today's word is that place: Ain Jalut.
screen: `A LETTER DEMANDING SURRENDER.` → `QUTUZ MARCHES NORTH.` → `A SPRING WITH AN OLD NAME.`

segments.voice: Start with the name. 'Ayn is Arabic for a spring, and also for an eye. Jalut is the name the Qur'an gives to Goliath. So Ain Jalut is the spring of Goliath. And the Qur'an tells that story, in surah al-Baqarah. A king called Talut, often identified with Saul, leads an army out against Jalut. He tests his men at a river: whoever drinks from it isn't with me, he says, except one who scoops up a single handful. Most of them drink. Only a few hold back. And that small group, facing Jalut's army, says, in Pickthall's English: "How many a little company hath overcome a mighty host by Allah's leave! Allah is with the steadfast." They ask Allah for patience and for firm feet. Then, the Qur'an says, David killed Goliath. Now the battle. The Mamluk army met the Mongols at that spring, and the Mamluks won. The Mongol advance toward Egypt stopped there. Among Qutuz's commanders was a man named Baybars. And history doesn't end tidily: the chronicles say that on the way home Qutuz was killed by his own officers, and Baybars became sultan. So why does the name matter? Because for the people who told this story, the place seemed to speak. A spring named for Goliath, where an army that had seemed unstoppable was stopped. In this story, the people Allah is with are the steadfast, the ones who hold their ground. Holding your ground isn't the same as winning every fight. It means there's a line, and you stay on it.
screen: `'AYN — A SPRING, OR AN EYE.` · `TALUT, JALUT, AND A LITTLE COMPANY.` · `THE MONGOLS STOPPED AT THE SPRING.` · `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.` · then, large: `THE SPRING OF GOLIATH.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand firm at one limit. Settle, and put both feet flat on the floor. Feel them there. Now think of one line in your life that keeps getting pushed: a habit you've said you'd stop, a request you keep saying yes to when you mean no, a boundary at work, with a phone, with a person. Name the line in a few words. Then picture the next time it gets tested, and see yourself staying on it, feet on the ground. If you pray, you can ask Allah for patience and firm feet, as the little company did. If you don't, simply hold the line in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ain Jalut. The spring of Goliath, in Palestine, where the Mamluks of Egypt stopped the Mongol advance. Today's word.
Your line: the spring of goliath. Today, when the line you named gets tested, feel your feet on the ground and stay on it once. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: The Mongols become Muslim
961.hook: within decades, Mongol rulers in Persia embrace Islam
961.howItsDone: Muslims tell the conversion of the Mongol rulers as a story of hearts turned, and the Prophet's prayer to the turner of hearts, asking for a heart kept firm in faith, is still said by Muslims today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ain Jalut, where the Mamluks stopped the Mongol advance, beside a spring named for Goliath. Your line was: the spring of goliath. Did you stay on your line when it was tested? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A Mongol prince stands in front of a gathering and takes a new name: Mahmud. His name until then was Ghazan. He is a descendant of Chinggis Khan, and he is reaching for the throne of Persia, the land his family's armies once overran. Rashid al-Din, who would serve him as vizier and write the history of the Mongols, describes him as raised a Buddhist. And now he declares himself a Muslim. Same family. Same throne. An heir of the storm from the east, praying toward Mecca. Today's words: the Mongols become Muslim.
screen: `A PRINCE TAKES A NEW NAME.` → `GHAZAN BECOMES MAHMUD.` → `THE STORM'S HEIR PRAYS.`

segments.voice: It wasn't only Ghazan. In the north, Berke, khan of the Golden Horde, had become Muslim before him. In Persia, after Ghazan, the Mongol rulers were Muslims, and they built mosques, endowed schools and gave scholars their patronage. The family whose armies had sacked Baghdad now ruled as Muslim kings. Hence the line: the conquerors converted. Here the people who won the war took up the faith of the people they had defeated. Why did it happen? Historians weigh it differently. Some stress faith, the plain story Rashid al-Din tells of a ruler who came to believe. Some stress politics: a king ruling a land full of mosques does well to pray in them. Some point to the scholars, Sufis and ordinary people around the court, whose lives showed the conquerors what Islam looked like. It's probably more than one of these at once. People are like that. And here's how the tradition itself talks about a change of heart. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that the hearts of people are between two of the fingers of the Most Merciful, and He turns them as He wills. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, another report says, often prayed asking the turner of hearts to keep his heart firm. Some tell this story as a reminder that no one's ending is known in advance.
screen: `BERKE IN THE NORTH, GHAZAN IN PERSIA.` · `THE WINNERS TOOK THE FAITH OF THE LOSERS.` · `FAITH, POLITICS, OR PEOPLE?` · `HEARTS BETWEEN TWO FINGERS.` · then, large: `THE CONQUERORS CONVERTED.`

segments.voice: The practice: believe change is possible. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you've quietly written off. A relative who will never change. A colleague you've filed under impossible. Or yourself, in one stubborn area. Hold them in mind without arguing for or against. Then ask yourself honestly: is the ending written yet? If you pray, you can ask Allah, the turner of hearts, to turn that heart, or yours, toward good. If you don't, simply leave the door in your mind open a crack, and let them stand in it. The bell holds the time.
The Mongols become Muslim. The rulers whose armies had swept through Persia and sacked Baghdad, taking up Islam, like Ghazan, who became Mahmud. Today's words.
Your line: the conquerors converted. Today, treat the person you'd written off as if their story isn't finished: one kind word, one fresh chance. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Al-Tusi's observatory
962.hook: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi builds an observatory at Maragha under Mongol rule
962.howItsDone: Muslims use the sky to set the times of prayer, the direction of Mecca and the months of the lunar calendar, and the sighting of the new moon marks the start and end of Ramadan for communities that follow local sighting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mongols become Muslim, and Ghazan takes the name Mahmud. Your line was: the conquerors converted. Did you give someone a fresh chance? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

On a hilltop above the town of Maragha, in Persia, workmen are laying stone for a building whose whole purpose is to watch the sky. Inside will go great instruments for measuring where the stars and planets stand, and a library to go with them. The money comes from Hulagu, the same Mongol prince whose army sacked Baghdad. And the man in charge is a Persian scholar, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. The storm that, the chroniclers say, drowned books in a river is now paying for star charts. Today's words: al-Tusi's observatory.
screen: `A HILLTOP ABOVE MARAGHA.` → `INSTRUMENTS AND A LIBRARY.` → `PAID FOR BY HULAGU.`

segments.voice: Al-Tusi was a scholar of many fields: astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, ethics, and the theology of the Shia tradition he belonged to. He came into Hulagu's service, and he persuaded the prince to build the observatory at Maragha. Scholars came to work there. They watched the sky night after night, measured, and wrote down tables of where the heavens moved, tables that astronomers went on using. And al-Tusi worked on a hard problem from the old Greek astronomy he had inherited: how to explain the planets' motions using only circles turning evenly. His answer is now called the Tusi couple. Picture a small circle rolling around inside a bigger one, twice as wide. A point on the small circle doesn't go round and round. It goes straight back and forth, in a line. Two circles, making a straight line. Some historians have noticed a very similar device in Copernicus's work, much later, and they still debate how it got there. So the line for today: learning survived. Not untouched. Not without a cost. But the habit of looking up and measuring carefully didn't die with Baghdad. It moved to a hilltop and kept going. Why would a believer care about tables of the stars? Partly for prayer: the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca are worked out from the sky. And partly because the Qur'an keeps pointing up. In surah Al 'Imran, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! In the creation of the heavens and the earth and (in) the difference of night and day are tokens (of His sovereignty) for men of understanding." For al-Tusi's circle, measuring the sky was one way of reading those tokens.
screen: `A SCHOLAR OF MANY FIELDS.` · `TABLES OF THE MOVING HEAVENS.` · `THE TUSI COUPLE: CIRCLES MAKE A LINE.` · `TOKENS FOR MEN OF UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `LEARNING SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the stars. If it's dark where you are, step outside or go to a window and look up. If it's daytime, look at the sky as it is, or close your eyes and remember the last night sky you really saw. Don't name anything. Just look. Notice how much is up there that you didn't put there, that keeps its own time without you. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can bring to mind the words the Qur'an gives just after that verse: our Lord, you did not create this in vain. If you don't, simply let the size of it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Al-Tusi's observatory. Built at Maragha under Mongol rule by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, a place to measure the sky after the fall of Baghdad. Today's words.
Your line: learning survived. Tonight, look up once before bed, and learn the name of one thing you see there: a star, a planet, the phase of the moon. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Mamluk Cairo
963.hook: former slave-soldiers rule Egypt and build mosques, hospitals and schools
963.howItsDone: Muslims speak of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, and some give to build or keep up mosques, schools, wells and hospitals in the hope that the good continues after them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Tusi's observatory on a hilltop at Maragha, paid for by a Mongol prince. Your line was: learning survived. Did you look up, and learn the name of one thing in the sky? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A boy is sold in a market far from home, somewhere on the grasslands north of the Black Sea. He is shipped to Egypt. There he is taught Arabic, the Qur'an and prayer, and then the horse, the bow and the lance. When his training ends, he is freed, and he becomes a soldier of the sultan. That was the path of the mamluks. Some boys who walked it ended up as sultans themselves, ruling Egypt from the citadel above Cairo. And then they started to build. Today's words: Mamluk Cairo.
screen: `A BOY SOLD FAR FROM HOME.` → `TRAINED, THEN FREED.` → `SOME BECAME SULTANS.`

segments.voice: In Arabic, mamluk means one who is owned. It's worth sitting with that word, because it's honest. These were children bought and taken from their families. Nothing in today's story makes that good. What the story shows is what some of them did once they held power. They built. Walk down the old main street of Cairo today and their buildings are still standing shoulder to shoulder: mosques, schools, fountains, tombs. Sultan Qalawun, who began as a mamluk himself, built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital, a bimaristan, side by side. The endowment that paid for the hospital, as historians describe it, was meant for anyone who was sick, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge. Later, Qalawun's grandson Sultan Hasan, born a prince rather than bought, built a great mosque and college, with space for teaching the different schools of Sunni law under one roof. Why build like this? Partly for memory and standing, like rulers anywhere. But there's a teaching underneath it, one taught in the very schools they built. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except three: a charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A hospital is a charity that keeps on giving. A school is knowledge that keeps being used. Men who had once been owned, and their heirs, may well have been thinking about what they would leave behind when they owned nothing again. Hence the line: slaves became builders. The stones are still there. People still pray in some of those mosques.
screen: `MAMLUK — ONE WHO IS OWNED.` · `QALAWUN: A TOMB, A SCHOOL, A HOSPITAL.` · `SULTAN HASAN'S MOSQUE AND COLLEGE.` · `THREE DEEDS THAT DON'T END.` · then, large: `SLAVES BECAME BUILDERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to visit an old building near you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the oldest building you can get to this week: a mosque, a church, a library, a town hall, a school, a bridge. Picture yourself at its door. Look for the details a hurried visitor misses: a step worn hollow by feet, a carved date or a name over the entrance, a patch where the stone has been mended. What was it built to do, and what does it do now? If you pray, you can ask that whatever good it still does keep going. If you don't, simply choose the day you'll go. The bell holds the time.
Mamluk Cairo. The city ruled by former slave-soldiers, who filled it with mosques, schools and hospitals that still stand. Today's words.
Your line: slaves became builders. This week, step inside one old building near you, look up at the ceiling for a moment, and find out one thing about who built it. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: Ibn Taymiyyah
964.hook: a Damascus scholar of the Mongol age, influential and debated, who called for return to early sources
964.howItsDone: Students of Islamic law and theology read Ibn Taymiyyah's fatwas and treatises alongside those of scholars who disagreed with him, and teachers stress reading each ruling with the question and setting that produced it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mamluk Cairo, where men who had once been owned built hospitals and schools. Your line was: slaves became builders. Which old building near you did you find? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

A question arrives at a scholar's door in Damascus. It concerns a town called Mardin. Its people are Muslims, but the power over them now belongs to the Mongols, whose armies have been raiding toward Syria. So which is it, the questioners want to know: a land of peace, or a land of war? The answer matters. It decides how people there are to be treated, and what they owe. The scholar gives an answer that fits neither box, and readers have argued over it ever since. His name is today's word: Ibn Taymiyyah.
screen: `A QUESTION ABOUT MARDIN.` → `PEACE OR WAR?` → `AN ANSWER STILL ARGUED OVER.`

segments.voice: Ibn Taymiyyah taught in Damascus in the age of the Mongol raids, a scholar of the Hanbali school, sharp, prolific, and not one to avoid a fight. His great call was to go back to the sources: the Qur'an, the Sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and the way of the earliest generations of Muslims, the salaf. Back past the layers, he argued, to the beginning. His answer on Mardin shows the kind of distinction he drew. He said the town was neither simply a land of peace nor simply a land of war. It was a third kind, a mixture. The Muslims living there were to be treated as Muslims, and those who had left the path were to be treated as their conduct deserved. The question offered two colors, and he refused to paint with only two. His life was not quiet. He clashed with rulers and with other scholars. He was imprisoned more than once, and his student Ibn Kathir records that he died a prisoner in the citadel of Damascus. Today his name is still argued over. Some Muslims call him Shaykh al-Islam and read him closely. Others, including theologians and Sufis, have disagreed with him sharply on important points. And in our own time, his words have been quoted for very different purposes, sometimes cut loose from their questions. That's why today's line is what it is: read him in his age. A ruling written for a town under Mongol power, by a man watching armies on the border, has to be read with that town and those armies in view. That's true of any scholar. Know the question before you judge the answer.
screen: `A SCHOLAR OF THE MONGOL AGE.` · `BACK TO THE SOURCES.` · `MARDIN: NOT PEACE, NOT WAR, A THIRD KIND.` · `ADMIRED, DEBATED, QUOTED.` · then, large: `READ HIM IN HIS AGE.`

segments.voice: The practice: read before judging. Settle, and breathe. Think of a writer, a scholar or a public figure you have strong feelings about, for or against, mostly from what other people say about them. Be honest: how much of their own words have you actually read? Now ask three questions about one thing they said. Who were they answering? When? What was happening around them? You may not know the answers. Just notice how much they'd change. If you pray, you can ask Allah for fairness in how you judge. If you don't, simply hold the questions. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Taymiyyah. A Damascus scholar of the Mongol age who called people back to the early sources, admired by some, debated by others. Today's word.
Your line: read him in his age. Today, before you share a quotation from anyone, find out when and why they said it. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

965.title: The first refuge was Africa
965.hook: the first Muslim refugees were welcomed in Abyssinia
965.howItsDone: Muslims tell the emigration to Abyssinia as the first hijrah, and the Negus's protection of the refugees is remembered in sermons and lessons about sheltering the persecuted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Taymiyyah, and his answer about Mardin: not peace, not war, a third kind. Your line was: read him in his age. Before you shared someone's words, did you ask when and why they said them? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

Umar ibn al-Khattab walks into his daughter Hafsah's house in Medina and finds a visitor there, a woman just back from across the sea. Her name is Asma bint Umays. When he learns where she has been, he tells her: we emigrated before you did, so we have more right to the Messenger of Allah than you. Asma doesn't laugh. She's angry. And she says she won't eat or drink until she has taken it to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Where had she been? The answer opens a new part of our road. Today's words: the first refuge was Africa.
screen: `UMAR TEASES A VISITOR.` → `WE EMIGRATED BEFORE YOU.` → `ASMA TAKES IT TO THE PROPHET.`

segments.voice: Asma had been in Abyssinia, across the Red Sea in East Africa. Years earlier, in Mecca, believers who were being persecuted had crossed that sea, and a Christian king, the Negus, had sheltered them. Asma and her husband Ja'far were among them. Before there was a Medina to go to, there was Africa. Now listen to what she says back to Umar, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in paraphrase. You were with the Prophet, she tells him. He fed your hungry and taught your ignorant. We were far away, among strangers, in a land where we were hated, and all of it for the sake of Allah and His Messenger. So she goes to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and tells him what Umar said. And he answers: Umar has no more right to me than you do. He and his companions made one hijrah. You, the people of the ship, made two. Two emigrations. One across the sea to Africa, and one from Africa to Medina. The Prophet counts the African years as a hijrah in their own right, not a detour. And the report adds one more detail. Abu Musa, who had sailed home with them, says that afterward the people of the ship came to Asma in groups to hear her tell it, and nothing in the world made them happier or meant more to them than what the Prophet had said. That's where the story of Islam in Africa begins: not with an army, but with refugees and a king who would not hand them over. Africa sheltered them first.
screen: `SHE HAD BEEN IN ABYSSINIA.` · `WE WERE FAR AWAY, AMONG STRANGERS.` · `YOU MADE TWO HIJRAHS.` · `THEY CAME TO HEAR HER TELL IT.` · then, large: `AFRICA SHELTERED THEM FIRST.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank a refuge. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place or a person that sheltered you when you needed it. A grandparent's house. A friend's sofa. A teacher's classroom at lunch. A country that took your family in. A mosque, a library, a kitchen where nobody asked questions. Let it come clearly: the door, the smell, the face. Stay there for a while, and let yourself be grateful. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward that person or that place. If you don't, simply say thank you in your head, and mean it. The bell holds the time.
The first refuge was Africa. Before Medina, believers fleeing Mecca were sheltered in Abyssinia, and the Prophet counted it as a hijrah. Today's words.
screen: `THE FIRST REFUGE WAS AFRICA — today's words`.

segments.voice: Your line: africa sheltered them first. Today, send one message of thanks to a person or a place that once sheltered you, even if it's years late. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

966.title: Egypt and the Nile
966.hook: Amr ibn al-As enters Egypt in 640, and over centuries Egypt becomes mostly Muslim
966.howItsDone: Muslims in Egypt pray in mosques old and new, including the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in Cairo, and live alongside Coptic Christian neighbors whose churches go back to before Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people of the ship, and the Prophet's word that they had made two hijrahs. Your line was: africa sheltered them first. Did you thank someone who once sheltered you? Day nine hundred sixty-six.

Remember the envoys from Mecca who sailed to Abyssinia with gifts for the Negus, hoping he'd hand the refugees back? Ibn Ishaq names one of them: Amr ibn al-As. He went home empty-handed. Later he became a Muslim himself, and a commander. And one day, under the caliph Umar, he leads an army west out of Palestine, across the edge of the desert, toward a green river valley that had been home to kings, temples and churches long before. Today's words: Egypt and the Nile.
screen: `AN ENVOY TO THE NEGUS.` → `NOW A MUSLIM COMMANDER.` → `WEST, TOWARD THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: Egypt in Arabic is Misr, the same name the Qur'an uses in the story of Yusuf, where Egypt is the land that takes him in and where, in the end, his whole family comes to live. When Amr's army arrived, Egypt was ruled from Constantinople, and in its towns and villages the Arab soldiers met Coptic Christians. Amr took the fortress beside the Nile, and later Alexandria by the sea. Then he founded a new town on the river bank, called Fustat, and built a mosque there. It has been rebuilt again and again, and it still carries his name: the mosque of Amr ibn al-As. Before any of this, a hadith in Sahih Muslim says, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his companions that they would one day enter Egypt, and asked them to treat its people well, because they had a claim of protection and of kinship. Scholars explain the kinship through Hajar, the mother of Ismail, and through Mariyah the Copt, the mother of the Prophet's son Ibrahim. And here is the part that's easy to get wrong. Egypt did not become Muslim when Amr arrived. Historians describe a slow change. Over generations, more and more Egyptians became Muslim, through marriage, through trade, through the pull of the cities, through taxes and law, through faith. Arabic slowly became the language of the street. And Coptic Christians stayed. They are still there, in their churches, and the old Coptic language is still sung in their liturgy. Hence the line: slowly, over centuries. A country's faith didn't change in a battle. It changed in kitchens and markets, one family at a time, across lifetimes.
screen: `MISR — THE LAND THAT TOOK YUSUF IN.` · `AMR, FUSTAT, AND A MOSQUE.` · `TREAT ITS PEOPLE WELL: PROTECTION AND KINSHIP.` · `COPTS STAYED, AND STILL SING.` · then, large: `SLOWLY, OVER CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: The practice: learn one Egyptian mosque. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the mosque of Amr ibn al-As in old Cairo: a broad open courtyard under the sky, rows of columns holding up the roof, the noise of the city outside its walls. Rebuilt again and again, and still in use, near the river where it began. Hold that picture: one building, prayed in by generations who each added a little. If you pray, you can make a dua for the people who pray there now. If you don't, simply hold the place in mind. The bell holds the time.
Egypt and the Nile. Misr, the land of Yusuf, which Amr ibn al-As entered, and where, slowly, families became Muslim beside Coptic neighbors. Today's words.
Your line: slowly, over centuries. Today, find one photo of the mosque of Amr ibn al-As, and notice one detail you didn't expect. Day nine hundred sixty-six.
